A hierarchy in which a central switch connects to other switches, each serving its own group of endpoints.
A cable layout that connects devices in a closed loop, including a connection from the last device back to the first.
A direct communication link joining exactly two devices.
An arrangement in which one central device communicates with multiple other devices and their communication passes through that center.
An arrangement of interconnected devices with redundant paths, implemented with connections between all pairs or only selected pairs.
The movement of a transmitted electrical or other network signal through the communication medium.
An electrical signal reaching an unterminated cable end and traveling back along the cable, potentially interfering with later signals.
A resistive component at the end of a legacy bus cable that absorbs signals to prevent them from returning along the cable.
The high-capacity connections used to carry traffic between LANs or between switches.
A radio-based point-to-point connection that links separate networks, such as the LANs in two buildings.
A shared-media arrangement in which connected stations hear transmissions and share the available bandwidth, even when the cabling forms a star.
A logical arrangement that creates temporary forwarding paths between source and destination ports so separate device pairs can communicate concurrently.
The central device in a token ring network whose internal electronics pass data around an ordered loop and bypass unused ports.
The rules an interface uses to access a medium and send frames, often specifying frame structure and acceptable media.
LAN cabling consisting of four pairs of copper wires twisted together inside a jacket, susceptible to electrical interference.
A medium that carries pulses of light through thin glass strands, supports long distances, and is immune to electrical interference.
The cable medium used for early physical-bus Ethernet and still used for cable TV and cable-modem Internet access.
Signaling that sends digital pulses using the medium's bandwidth for one transmission, as described for Ethernet LANs.
Signaling that divides a medium into separate frequency channels so it can carry multiple signals, as in cable TV and cable Internet.
A 48-bit physical identifier of a network interface, commonly written as twelve hexadecimal digits.
The unit of network information transmitted and received by NICs and forwarded by switches, containing a header, data, and a trailer.
The four-byte Ethernet trailer field that stores an error-checking value for detecting damage in transit.
A mathematically calculated error-detection value that a receiver recomputes and compares with the transmitted value to detect altered data.
The rules governing how and when a network interface may transmit onto a communication medium.
The half-duplex Ethernet access algorithm that listens before transmitting, detects simultaneous transmissions, and retries after a random wait.
acceptedTerms: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection

questions.definition: An event in which two or more devices transmit simultaneously onto the same shared medium and their signals interfere.
The shared Ethernet segment or group of hub-connected segments across which interfering simultaneous transmissions can propagate, bounded by switch or router ports.
Communication in which a station can send and receive data, but cannot do both at the same time.
Communication in which a station can send and receive at the same time; on a switched Ethernet link, collision detection is unnecessary.
An Ethernet variant providing 10 Mbps over Category 3 or higher twisted-pair cabling using two wire pairs.
The common 100 Mbps twisted-pair Ethernet variant that uses two wire pairs, one for sending and one for receiving.
A 100 Mbps fiber-based Ethernet variant useful for backbone links, longer cable runs, and electrically noisy locations.
The twisted-pair Gigabit Ethernet variant that uses all four pairs and can transmit and receive on each pair simultaneously.
The paired Ethernet options providing 2.5 and 5 Gbps on existing Cat 5e/6 cabling, useful for faster access-point uplinks.
The full-duplex-only 10 Gbps twisted-pair Ethernet variant described as using four pairs of Cat 6A or Cat 7 cabling.
The IEEE 802.11 family of networking technologies that carries local network traffic using radio signals.
A location offering access to a public wireless LAN, such as a library or cafe.
A wireless operating mode in which stations connect through a central access point before communicating with other devices.
A wireless operating mode in which devices communicate directly without a central access point, often for small or temporary installations.
An antenna that covers surrounding devices in a broad pattern, typically strongest horizontally around its axis and weaker above and below it.
An antenna that focuses radio energy in one direction, useful for a narrow space or a link between buildings.
The wireless access algorithm that listens for the medium, seeks to avoid simultaneous transmissions, and uses acknowledgments and retry delays for unsuccessful exchanges.
acceptedTerms: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance

questions.definition: The 802.11 access method described as using a collision-avoidance algorithm to coordinate stations sharing the wireless medium.
A waiting interval before retrying transmission; the chapter describes a random delay after an unsuccessful wireless exchange.
A wireless condition in which clients can reach the access point but cannot hear each other, so their transmissions may interfere without mutual awareness.
The initial control message a wireless station sends to ask an access point for permission to transmit when optional handshaking is enabled.
The control reply granting a wireless station permission to transmit after it asks the access point, allowing other stations to defer.
A reduction in signal strength, such as the weakening that occurs when radio waves pass through dense material.
A process in which material takes in radio signal energy, leaving a weaker signal after it passes through the material.
The bending of a radio wave as it passes between media of different densities, changing its direction of travel.
The bending of a wave around an obstacle, which can distort the wave or redirect part of it.
The bouncing of a radio wave from a dense reflective surface, creating a copy that may follow a different path to the receiver.
The unpredictable redirection of radio energy by small irregular objects such as leaves, dust, or water droplets.
The arrival of copies of the same radio signal along different routes and at different times, potentially causing distortion.
A comparison of useful signal strength with the level of background interference affecting reception.
The actual data transfer rate after accounting for losses to errors and acknowledgments, before excluding protocol headers from the delivered data.
The rate at which useful application data is delivered, excluding protocol headers and other network overhead.
Network traffic beyond the application content, including packet and frame headers, acknowledgments, and retransmissions.
An antenna technique that uses multiple separately processed signal paths or data streams to improve wireless capacity, introduced in 802.11n.
A wireless capability that lets an access point send data to several client stations at the same time.
A technique that directs an access point's radio transmission toward a receiving device instead of spreading it uniformly in all directions.
The IEEE 802.5 LAN technology that usually uses physical star cabling while passing a special permission frame around a logical loop.
A controlled access method in which a special frame circulates between stations and only its current holder may transmit data.
A legacy 100 Mbps networking technology that uses token passing and usually two fiber-optic rings for redundancy.

questions.prompt: A switch receives a unicast frame on port 4 from a MAC address it has never seen. What does it learn from that frame?
options: The destination MAC address belongs to port 4.
The sender's IP address belongs to port 4.
The source MAC address belongs to port 4.
The source MAC address belongs to every port in the VLAN.
questions.explanation: The switch learns the source MAC address and associates it with the port that received the frame.

questions.prompt: A switch has no table entry for a frame's unicast destination. How does it forward the frame?
options: It returns the frame to the sender.
It sends the frame out the other forwarding ports in the same VLAN.
It sends the frame only to a router's port.
It waits for the aging time to expire before sending the frame.
questions.explanation: An unknown unicast is flooded within its VLAN. The switch excludes the ingress port.

questions.prompt: A server disconnects and stops sending frames. What eventually removes its dynamically learned MAC entry from the switch table?
questions.explanation: A dynamic entry expires when frames from its source MAC address have not refreshed it within the aging interval.

questions.prompt: A technician checks a copper Ethernet link. Which statements describe features discussed in the chapter? Select all correct answers.
options: Autonegotiation can select a speed and duplex mode supported by both ends.
Full-duplex requires devices to take turns transmitting.
Auto-MDIX can swap the transmit and receive pin assignments as needed.
Full-duplex allows both ends to transmit at the same time.
questions.explanation: Autonegotiation resolves link speed and duplex, auto-MDIX adapts to the cable pairing, and full-duplex allows simultaneous transmission and reception.

questions.prompt: Match each switching method to the amount of the frame it inspects before forwarding.

pairs.definition: Reads the addressing information and starts forwarding before receiving the complete frame.
Reads enough to check for an undersized frame without checking the full frame for errors.
Buffers the full frame and verifies its frame check sequence.

questions.explanation: The methods trade forwarding latency for how thoroughly they can check the frame.

questions.prompt: A switch must reject damaged frames that are still a valid size and fail the frame check sequence. Which forwarding method can do this?
questions.explanation: Valid-size frames can still be corrupted. Store-and-forward checks the complete frame before sending it on.

questions.prompt: A multicast video stream should reach only ports with interested receivers. What can a managed switch use to make that forwarding decision?
questions.explanation: IGMP snooping lets a switch track multicast group membership and limit multicast forwarding to the relevant ports.

questions.prompt: Two access switches have redundant links. Explain how spanning tree prevents a switching loop while keeping an alternate path available.
questions.exampleAnswer: Spanning tree leaves a loop-free set of forwarding paths by blocking a redundant path. If an active link fails, it recalculates which ports can forward and can put the alternate path into service.

questions.prompt: A campus with redundant switch links needs faster recovery to a loop-free topology after a link failure. Which spanning-tree enhancement addresses that need?
questions.explanation: Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol converges faster after a topology change than traditional Spanning Tree Protocol.

questions.prompt: An edge port intended for a workstation receives a spanning-tree control frame from a newly connected switch. Which protection can disable that edge port?
questions.explanation: BPDU Guard protects an edge port by disabling it when it receives a spanning-tree control frame.

questions.prompt: A project has staff on several floors. They should share one broadcast domain, while other staff on those floors should be in a different broadcast domain. Which feature supports this design?
questions.explanation: VLAN membership lets the switch group ports into logical broadcast domains independently of physical location.

questions.prompt: On an IEEE 802.1Q trunk, the _____ identifies the VLAN associated with a tagged Ethernet frame.
questions.explanation: The tag lets a device on the far end of a trunk associate the frame with the proper VLAN.

questions.prompt: Two hosts are connected to the same multilayer switch and are assigned to different VLANs with different IP subnets. What capability lets the switch carry traffic between them?
questions.explanation: A multilayer switch can route IP packets between the VLANs. Ordinary Layer 2 forwarding stays within a VLAN.

questions.prompt: A lab has dedicated workstation jacks. The administrator wants a switch port to allow only the assigned device's MAC address. Which option fits?
options: Put every workstation in the same VLAN.
Apply switch port security to the port.
Set the port to store-and-forward switching.
Aggregate the port with the uplink.
questions.explanation: Switch port security can limit the number and identity of MAC addresses allowed on a port.

questions.prompt: A busy uplink needs more combined capacity for several simultaneous conversations. Both switches support bundling their physical interfaces. Which feature should the administrator use?
questions.explanation: Link aggregation combines multiple physical links into one logical connection with greater aggregate capacity.

questions.prompt: Match each switch interface or feature to its job.

pairs.definition: Provides power and a data connection over the same Ethernet cable.
Accepts an interchangeable interface module for compatible fiber or copper media.
Provides a direct management connection for initial configuration.

questions.explanation: A switch can use different ports for powered endpoints, replaceable network interfaces, and local management.

questions.prompt: Two IP networks are joined by a router. A workstation sends an Ethernet broadcast intended for its own LAN. What happens at the router?
options: The router floods the Ethernet frame into both networks.
The broadcast frame stays on the originating LAN.
The router adds a VLAN tag and forwards it into the other network.
The router replaces the source MAC address and floods it out the other interface.
questions.explanation: A router separates Layer 2 broadcast domains, so it does not forward the original local Ethernet broadcast to another network.

questions.prompt: A router forwards an IP packet over an Ethernet link to another router. What destination MAC address goes in the outgoing Ethernet frame?
options: The destination host's MAC address on its remote subnet
The next router's MAC address on the outgoing link
The forwarding router's outgoing MAC address
questions.explanation: The router builds a new Ethernet frame for the outgoing link. On a route through another router, that next hop is the Ethernet destination.

questions.prompt: Match the routing table information to what it tells an administrator.

pairs.definition: The network prefix covered by the route.
The next router or outgoing interface used to continue toward the destination.
The numeric path cost under the route's selection rules.
The router's preference for a route source when sources offer a route to the same prefix.

questions.explanation: Destination, forwarding information, path cost, and source preference answer different questions about a route.

questions.prompt: An engineer assigns an IP address to an active router interface. The subnet attached to that interface appears in the routing table without a routing protocol or manual route entry. How was the route derived?
options: It was advertised by an exterior gateway protocol.
It was entered as a static route.
It was learned from a distance-vector neighbor.
questions.explanation: An active interface allows the router to reach its attached subnet directly.

questions.prompt: If no more specific route matches a packet's destination, the router can use its _____, if one is present.
questions.explanation: A default route is the fallback for destinations that have no more specific match.

questions.prompt: A router uses RIP. Path A reaches a destination in one hop over a slower link. Path B reaches the same destination in two hops over faster links. Which path does RIP prefer?
options: Path A, because it has fewer hops.
Path B, because its links have greater bandwidth.
Both paths, because they reach the same destination.
Path B, because it passes through more routers.
questions.explanation: RIP uses hop count. Faster links do not change the RIP metric.

questions.prompt: Two internal paths reach the same destination. The two-hop path has total configured OSPF cost 12, and the one-hop path has cost 30. Which path does OSPF prefer?
options: The one-hop path, because it passes through fewer routers.
Both paths, because they connect the same networks.
The two-hop path, because it has lower total cost.
The one-hop path, because its cost is higher.
questions.explanation: OSPF uses the total path cost, so the route with cost 12 wins.

questions.prompt: Which of these are link-state routing protocols discussed in Chapter 8? Select all correct answers.
questions.explanation: OSPF and IS-IS calculate paths using link-state information. RIPv2 is distance-vector and BGP is path-vector.

questions.prompt: After an uplink fails, which observation best shows that the routing network has converged?
options: A router has started sending an update about the failed link.
The routers have updated their routing information to reflect the failed link and the available paths.
The timestamps on every route have reached the same value.
Every router now has the same next hop for each destination.
questions.explanation: Convergence occurs when routing information has settled after a topology change. Routers can legitimately use different next hops.

questions.prompt: A company needs to exchange routes with an ISP in a separate autonomous system. Which protocol from the chapter is designed for this role?
questions.explanation: BGP exchanges routing information between autonomous systems. OSPF, IS-IS, and RIPv2 are interior gateway protocols.

questions.prompt: A router can advertise one larger network prefix in place of several more specific prefixes it covers. What technique is this?
questions.explanation: Route summarization represents several network destinations with a single, less specific routing entry.

questions.prompt: A growing network relies on manually configured routes and now has a backup link between sites. Why could traffic still stop after the primary route fails, and what change could reduce downtime?
questions.exampleAnswer: A router that relies solely on the manually configured primary route may have no alternate route to use even when a backup link is working. A dynamic routing protocol can learn the backup route and recalculate paths after the failure.

questions.prompt: An administrator wants a router to allow traffic to a server subnet from only an approved client subnet and for only an approved protocol. Which ACL fields help express the policy? Select all correct answers.
options: Link speed in megabits per second
questions.explanation: An ACL can filter by source and destination addresses and by protocol. The administrator also chooses the interface and direction where the rule applies.

questions.prompt: A new enterprise switch has no management IP address configured. Which connection does the chapter describe for initial local setup?
options: An Ethernet connection to a trunk port
A link to an SFP data port
A terminal emulator connected to the console port
A wireless connection using the switch's SSID
questions.explanation: A local console session provides direct access to the Cisco IOS command line before network management is configured.

questions.prompt: Match each Cisco IOS prompt to the work available in that mode.

pairs.definition: View basic status information using a limited command set.
Use the elevated EXEC command set to inspect the running configuration.
Change settings that affect the device as a whole.

questions.explanation: The prompt distinguishes user EXEC, privileged EXEC, and global configuration mode.

questions.prompt: A technician wants to see which MAC addresses a Cisco switch learned and the interfaces associated with them. Which read-only command gives that information?
questions.explanation: The MAC address table lists learned MAC addresses and the switch interfaces associated with them.

questions.prompt: Which read-only Cisco IOS command displays networks known to a router and how to reach them?
questions.explanation: The routing table displayed by show ip route contains destination routes and their forwarding information.

questions.prompt: An administrator is reviewing a change that must survive a reboot. Which configuration should contain the saved change?
options: The running configuration in RAM only
questions.explanation: The running configuration contains the active settings. The startup configuration stores the settings that are loaded at boot.

questions.prompt: Which are basic wireless settings on the access point described in the chapter? Select all correct answers.
questions.explanation: Network name, radio mode, and channel define aspects of how clients discover or connect to the wireless network.

questions.prompt: An access point and all client devices support WEP, WPA, WPA2, and WPA3. Which option provides the strongest protection of those listed?
questions.explanation: WPA3 is the strongest of the four security protocols compared in the chapter.

questions.prompt: A campus Wi-Fi network checks each user's credentials against a central authentication service. Which protocol does the chapter associate with this arrangement?
questions.explanation: RADIUS lets an access point use a central service for enterprise authentication.

questions.prompt: A café wants guests to have internet access while preventing guests on the same wireless access point from communicating directly with each other. Which feature addresses this?
questions.explanation: AP isolation separates wireless clients so their traffic cannot go directly to each other through the access point.

questions.prompt: An office wants a private Wi-Fi network and a guest Wi-Fi network on the same access point. Explain how multiple SSIDs and VLAN support help separate their traffic on the wired network.
questions.exampleAnswer: The access point can publish a separate SSID for each wireless network and associate each SSID with a different wired VLAN. This lets the same access point place staff and guest traffic in separate broadcast domains.

questions.prompt: Match the wireless setting or mode to its purpose.

pairs.definition: Extends an existing wireless network's coverage.
Connects two physically separate wired networks over a wireless link.
Changes the strength of the access point's transmitted signal.

questions.explanation: These options solve different problems involving coverage, connectivity between sites, and signal range.

questions.prompt: Battery-powered sensors send brief readings periodically. Which Wi-Fi feature coordinates times for their radios to wake and exchange traffic?
questions.explanation: Target Wake Time schedules wake periods so clients can sleep between traffic exchanges and conserve power.

questions.prompt: The Wi-Fi feature that divides a channel into smaller resource units so multiple clients can use it efficiently is called _____.
questions.explanation: OFDMA allocates parts of the same radio channel to different clients during a transmission opportunity.

questions.prompt: Two network adapters use the same PCIe generation. One is labeled x4 and the other x1. What does x4 specify?
questions.explanation: The number after x is the lane count. At the same PCIe generation, more lanes offer greater potential bus bandwidth.

questions.prompt: A technician needs to add a network adapter to a laptop without opening its case. Which interface from the chapter suits an external adapter?
questions.explanation: A USB network adapter connects to an external port and can be added without opening the computer.

questions.prompt: Traffic arrives in bursts at a server's network adapter faster than the adapter can process it. Which NIC feature temporarily holds the incoming data?
questions.explanation: Extra buffer memory gives the NIC temporary space for traffic when it is arriving faster than it can be processed.

questions.prompt: A network adapter initiates data transfers across the computer's bus to system memory without asking the CPU to manage each transfer. Which feature enables that?
questions.explanation: With bus mastering, the adapter can manage transfers to and from system memory while the CPU does other work.

questions.prompt: Match each NIC feature or design to the requirement it serves.

pairs.definition: Automatically moves traffic to a standby connection when the primary connection fails.
Combines multiple links for more aggregate bandwidth.
Lets supported hardware be installed or removed while the server remains powered on.

questions.explanation: Failover maintains connectivity, aggregation increases combined capacity, and hot plugging helps service the hardware while the server runs.

questions.prompt: A server sends large backups while carrying live voice traffic. Which adapter feature helps give the time-sensitive voice traffic priority?
questions.explanation: Quality of service can assign higher transmission priority to time-sensitive traffic such as voice.

questions.prompt: An administrator wants to wake a sleeping PC remotely by sending a special network packet. The feature is called _____.
questions.explanation: Wake-on-LAN enables a compatible network adapter to recognize a special packet and signal the computer to wake.

questions.prompt: A diskless workstation needs to start using boot software delivered from the network. Which feature supports that requirement?
questions.explanation: PXE lets a computer obtain boot software over the network before its operating system starts.

questions.definition: An Ethernet switching device with administrator-configurable options, such as individual link speeds, VLANs, and security settings.
A connection setting that lets Ethernet devices exchange capabilities and automatically agree on a shared link speed and duplex setting.
A port feature that automatically swaps Ethernet transmit and receive pairs when needed so either a crossover or straight-through cable can be used.
A switch's learned record of which ports lead to specific hardware addresses.
The inactivity period after which a switch removes a dynamically learned MAC address from its forwarding table.
A method that starts sending an incoming frame once the switch has read enough of its header to choose an outgoing port.
A method that reads enough of an incoming frame to reject one shorter than the network's minimum frame length before forwarding.
A method that buffers an entire incoming frame and verifies its frame check sequence before sending it onward.
A switch feature that examines multicast membership messages to decide which ports should receive a multicast stream.
An overwhelming volume of Ethernet broadcasts that can arise when switches forward the same frames repeatedly through a Layer 2 loop.
The Ethernet protocol in which switches exchange information to prevent Layer 2 loops by keeping redundant paths from forwarding until needed.
The enhancement to the original IEEE 802.1D Ethernet loop-prevention protocol that restores a usable forwarding topology more quickly after a link changes.
A spanning-tree protection that disables an edge port if it receives a spanning-tree control frame.
A logical Layer 2 broadcast domain whose members can be grouped independently of their physical location.
A switch interface that carries traffic for multiple logical broadcast domains over one link, using tags to identify the domain a frame belongs to.
A managed Ethernet feature that can restrict the number or identity of MAC addresses allowed on a specific physical interface.
The combination of multiple physical network links into one logical connection with greater total capacity.
A technology that supplies electrical power and data to a device such as an access point over the same network cable.
A removable transceiver that fits a compatible switch or router slot and adapts the interface to a supported fiber or copper connection.
A device that combines ordinary Layer 2 frame switching with Layer 3 routing, often to connect VLANs internally.
The act of moving a received network-layer data unit to the outgoing router interface selected for its destination.
The forwarding target identified in a routing entry, typically the IP address of the immediately following router.
A numeric measure that a routing protocol uses to compare paths, based on factors such as link cost or the number of routers traversed.
A router's numeric preference for the source of a route, where a lower value indicates greater trust for routes to the same prefix.
A routing table entry representing a network attached to one of the router's own interfaces.
A path entry manually specified by an administrator instead of learned from another router.
The routing entry used when the destination IP address matches no more specific route.
A class of routing protocols in which routers share known routes and their costs with neighbors, without building a map of the full topology.
A distance-vector routing protocol family that judges routes solely by hop count and includes an original version and a second version.
A class of routing protocols in which routers distribute information about their interfaces and use a map of the topology to calculate routes.
A link-state interior gateway protocol that builds a topology map and selects paths based on accumulated interface costs.
The process by which routers reach a consistent view of network reachability after a topology change.
An internetwork under one organization's administration for routing purposes.
The path-vector routing protocol that exchanges network reachability between autonomous systems on the Internet.
A set of permit or deny rules on a router interface that can evaluate traffic by addresses, protocol, and direction.
A dedicated management interface that provides local command-line access to a switch or router for tasks such as initial configuration.
The initial Cisco IOS command mode with a prompt ending in > and access to a limited set of status commands.
The higher-access Cisco IOS command mode with a prompt ending in # that permits operations such as viewing the running configuration.
The Cisco IOS mode indicated by (config)# in which commands can change device-wide settings such as the hostname.
The configured wireless network name a client selects or enters when joining a Wi-Fi network.
The third-generation Wi-Fi security protocol and the strongest of the four compared in the chapter.
The protocol a wireless access point can use to ask a central server to verify a user's credentials for enterprise Wi-Fi access.
A wireless setting that keeps connected clients from communicating with one another while allowing them to reach the internet.
An access point mode that relays traffic for an existing wireless network to extend its coverage.
An access point mode in which a radio link connects physically separate wired networks, such as LANs in two buildings.
A Wi-Fi feature that schedules when battery-powered clients leave their sleep state to communicate, improving power and airtime efficiency.
The Wi-Fi feature that divides one channel into smaller frequency units so it can serve several clients at once.
A high-speed serial connection for internal devices that can combine lanes, with labels such as x4 indicating the number of lanes.
A NIC feature that uses memory to hold incoming or outgoing data temporarily when it arrives faster than it can be handled.
A NIC capability to initiate transfers to and from computer memory across the system bus without the CPU managing each transfer.
The automatic transfer of network traffic to a standby adapter when the primary adapter fails.
A power-management feature that lets a supported computer resume or power on after it receives a specially formatted network packet.
A network boot feature that lets a computer obtain startup software from a server without relying on an operating system already installed on a local drive.
Mechanisms that give time-sensitive traffic such as voice a higher delivery priority than less time-sensitive traffic.
